newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Lull in Afghan fighting as ceasefire hopes fade.
newsitem.headline: Lull in Afghan fighting as ceasefire hopes fade.

text.p: Warring Afghan factions pounded each other with artillery, mortars and rockets for several hours on Thursday before an unusual afternoon silence descended on the plain north of Kabul.

Fighters of the purist Islamic Taleban ruling the capital said the front line had not moved for the third day running despite a series of attacks on Wednesday by ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.

Masood commander Najim Khan told Reuter correspondent Chris Bird what had been branded a major offensive on Wednesday had failed to shift the Taleban from the De Sabz pass some 30 km (20 miles) north of Kabul.
"We are in the same positions we were last night," he said of the fighting on the east side of the plain.
The Taleban fighters near the front line village of Hussein Kot, 20 km (12 miles) from Kabul on the western side, told Reuters there had been no clashes with Masood forces on Thursday.
The artillery and rocket duels had been fought across the plain with the anti-Taleban forces to the east, they said.
Shells were lobbed on to Masood's positions below Khair Khana pass around 15 km (10 miles) north of Kabul on Thursday, witnesses reported.
A Taleban warplane also bombed the village of Kalakan at 9.15 a.m. (0445 GMT), hitting three houses.
Lines of women, their faces covered in long blue or yellow veils, and their children fled narrow village streets on foot.
"Why are they (Taleban) fighting women and children?" said Abdul Wahid, distraught after the bombing and leading his children out of the village.

The Taleban said the fighting would go on, adding to the views of Afghan watchers in Kabul, who said ceasefire talks appeared near collapse, making a new push on Kabul by anti-Taleban forces increasingly likely.
"Our understanding is that their positions are still far apart and the gap appears unbridgeable," said one veteran Afghan watcher.
"It looks like it's a question of when rather than whether they collapse and if they do then a significant offensive down the plain to Kabul seems inevitable," he said.
Ceasefire talks have been brokered by Pakistani Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar and United Nations Special Envoy Norbert Holl.
Holl saw northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum in his stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif on Wednesday and was to fly to Kandahar, the Taleban headquarters, on Thursday.
He appeared to have only slim hopes of pulling off a ceasefire, with Dostum and Masood demanding Kabul be demilitarised. The Taleban rejected that as unacceptable.
"Success is far from being guaranteed," Holl said after talking to Dostum.
"I suspect that's diplomatic language for there's little hope," said the Afghan watcher.

Another Afghan watcher with a military background said all the signs on the ground were that a major battle was likely on the plain north of Kabul, where Dostum sent tanks, artillery and men to join Masood's front line last week.

"The fact is that if Masood and Dostum move together, they probably have the strength to punch through the Taleban lines on both sides of the plain and drive all the way to Kabul," said an analyst with a military background.

Whether Dostum has sent his ground forces into action is not yet clear, and the Taleban say there is no evidence that he has. If he did, they say, he would be regarded as an enemy rather than someone they can do business with.
"It seems to me that the only question left is whether Masood and Dostum will actually try to take the city," the analyst said.

He and others said that if Masood did try to take the city he would create another bloodbath in a city marked by ruins from previous factional battles and that he would probably not want to squander popular support by doing so.

"He would simply put himself back in the position he was a month ago, sitting in the city with the Taleban in the hills round the southern edges of the valley and capable of rocketing it to pieces," said one. "I suspect he doesn't want that."
